thread.title: Riding The Tech Bull To Riches - Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:VGT)

author: Harry Sauers
title: Riding The Tech Bull To Riches - Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:VGT)
text:
I’ve been interested in technology investment as far back as I can remember; I read books like Founders at Work through my elementary school years and actually bought a share of Nintendo (regretfully) at the ripe old age of 10. The tech sector has been at the forefront of innovation and wealth creation for years now, as well as the center of news headlines during events such as the Consumer Electronics Show and the release of the latest iPhone. From the brilliant marketing and margins of Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) to the revolutionary success of Amazon’s (NASDAQ: AMZN ) growth into a true conglomerate, technology is clearly central to the future of wealth creation and offers great risk-adjusted potential.
However, traditional valuation metrics for the sector are limited at best and often cause investors to miss out on groundbreaking innovation, especially in areas such as AI, robotics, genomics, and information technology. The success of Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), Amazon, and the broad biotech sector in recent years are fantastic examples of this - as a result of their relative low profitability in a market prone to speculation, many investors were left feeling as if they missed out. Due to the more speculative nature of tech, investors must have an exceptionally strong confidence in the future of technology - and would do well to avoid trying to pick out individual stocks, particularly in their earlier stages.
Here, we will explore several technology ETFs and closed-end funds so as to take a bullish stance on tech into the future. The time horizon, as I use for all of my investments, is 10+ years. In that timeframe, we may see major downturns and recessions ( the NASDAQ 100 famously fell 78% from its peak during the dotcom bubble) but so long as we watch for glaring signs of a bubble sector-wide, the core thesis remains intact.
I am a strong believer that artificial intelligence and our ongoing technological revolution will continue for decades to come at an accelerating pace. If that belief is proven wrong there will be no safe haven for money - but if I’m right, shareholders will be very, very happy some years from now.
Some investors may choose a value approach. TDIV , the ETF issued by First Trust, is a dividend-weighted index of technology and telecommunications stocks. As such, it is heavily weighted towards big names like Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ), Apple, IBM (NYSE: IBM ), and Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO ). Though many of these are solid plays, it is nothing special, but may certainly offer an edge to the risk-averse seeking exposure to the tech sector. Warren Buffett might be a fan of this ETF’s theme, as it plays into his “boring” and value-oriented investment style. Holding an expense ratio of 0.50%, it’s nothing to write home about but is certainly not as bad as the speculative ARKW (with an expense ratio of 1%).
For most, however, simple cap-weighted indexes serve this purpose equally well, provided one can stomach a bit more risk and less income. I personally opted for XLK due to its broad exposure, lower P/E ratio relative to its peers, and low expense ratio. Other options include VGT , QTEC , and FTEC - each holding their own unique risks, rewards, and characteristics.
Portfolio Core QQQ:
Though not a pure tech ETF, the QQQ is worthy of mention in any discussion of technology funds. Two-thirds of the fund by market cap is devoted to information technology companies, and it tracks the Nasdaq 100 index. The QQQ offers investors a respectable 0.20% expense ratio, but over time has been shown to be more volatile than the S&P 500 and may not offer the small-cap or total-market exposure sought.
IXN:
For those seeking a global edge to their tech portfolio, IXN is an excellent vehicle for this. Though, like most cap-weighted ETFs, it is overweight in Apple, names such as Tencent Holdings ( OTCPK:TCEHY ), Alibaba (NYSE: BABA ), and Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE: TSM ) are also noteworthy in this fund’s top holdings. The expense ratio is 0.48%.
XLK:
State Street’s Technology Select Sector ETF is quite similar to the QQQ, minus non-tech stocks. It is almost entirely large-cap, and unfortunately does have notable concentration risk with just two of its holdings - Apple and Microsoft - comprising over 25% of the portfolio. It should be paired with a fund like RYT or PSCT if an investor is seeking to have broad exposure, but XLK is quite good at tracking the biggest names in tech at the low cost of 0.13%.
VGT:
No sector profile would be complete without a reference to one of Vanguard’s funds. Known for their remarkably low expense ratios (0.10% in this case) and excellent diversification, the Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEARCA: VGT ) is a total-market fund for U.S. tech stocks. Though its top holdings are overweight in the portfolio, about 15% is dedicated to mid, small, and micro-cap stocks to balance this out.
QTEC:
QTEC is hardly worthy of mention, given that it tracks the same benchmark as XLK at four times the expense ratio (0.53%). It is good at limiting single-company exposure with the largest holding, Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT ), taking up a mere 2.42%, but the limited scope and nonsensical management choices make this fund mediocre.
FTEC:
The Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF (NYSEARCA: FTEC ) has the lowest expense ratio of all the funds we will examine, weighing in at a mere 0.08%. It is somewhat better than the aforementioned funds at reducing single-company risk, and provides broad exposure with holdings ranging from Visa (NYSE: V ) to Texas Instruments (NYSE: TXN ) to Google. It also offers a similar smaller-cap exposure to its Vanguard equivalent, with about 14% of holdings in mid-cap and smaller companies.
RYT:
RYT is a very interesting play in the world of tech ETFs. It tracks companies in the S&P 500 in the information technology sector, and weights each one equally, regardless of market cap or any other methodology. This leads to a full quarter of holdings to be dedicated to mid-cap companies in the S&P, which other funds often overlook. However, it doesn’t come cheap: its expense ratio is 0.40% annually. I highly recommend this ETF as a means to nearly eliminate single-company risk, which is a major factor in technology indexing.
PSCT:
The Invesco S&P SmallCap Information Technology ETF (NASDAQ: PSCT ) tracks publicly traded equities in the tech sector and belonging to the S&P Small Cap 600 index. This allows for good diversification within the sector, but due to the high failure rate of small-cap tech it does not offer meaningful returns when compared to the risk, even with its expense ratio of just 0.29%. Investors would be better off gaining small-cap exposure through a vehicle such as HTGC, which is an actively managed BDC focusing on early-stage technology and biomedical investment.
Though the performance of thematic ETFs has remained unproven over long periods of time, the recent trend towards niche ETFs is noteworthy. These generally come with higher expense ratios than simple index funds, and are sometimes actively managed. They carry greater risk than broad index funds in a variety of ways: sector, company concentration, and notably liquidity risk. However, for those with a healthy appetite for risk, they may offer exposure to smaller-cap companies with greater innovative potential and future prospects. I advise against a large allocation to any of these.
Special Additions
ROBT:
ROBT is my favorite of the three major robotics and automation ETFs, clocking in with an expense ratio of 0.65% annually. Its managers opted for a unique weighting system of three categories: “Engagers,” “Enablers,” and “Enhancers.” These categories are weighted at 60%, 25%, and 15% of the fund, respectively, and thirty companies are selected within each and weighted equally. Drawing from the prospectus , companies “are classified into one of three categories: enablers (companies in advance machinery, semiconductors, or databases used for machine learning), engagers (companies offering products, software, or systems), or enhancers (companies that provide value to the industry but AI/Robotics is not the core business).” Because I am a risk-on investor with regards to tech and automation, I quite like the equal-weighting approach to this fund and have a minor position in my portfolio. Investors should note that this fund is only a few months old and is unproven over time, and may be fairly illiquid.
BOTZ:
The Global X Robotics & Artificial Intelligence ETF (NASDAQ: BOTZ ) is more well-known in this arena and selects holdings based on companies that “earn a significant portion of their revenue from, or have a stated business purpose in, the field of robotics or artificial intelligence .” It is market cap-weighted, and significantly overweight towards Japan, while dedicating just 29% of its holdings to American companies. These holdings are not hedged by currency, but may offer investors access to a specific market overlooked by other funds. BOTZ has an expense ratio of 0.68%, which is about average for thematic ETFs.
ROBO:
ROBO is the original Robotics and Automation ETF, and has had the opportunity to demonstrate longer-term performance of its investments. Like its sister funds, there is a heavy weight given to Japan and the U.S. Despite this, it is well-diversified for this specialized sector, and has 88 holdings weighted by market cap selected by the ROBO index committee. Its expense ratio of a whopping 0.95% makes it a hard sell for those with a long-term horizon, though it is possible that risk-adjusted performance will make up for it. This expense ratio puts me off from holding it in my portfolio.
EMQQ:
The Emerging Markets Internet & Ecommerce ETF (NYSEARCA: EMQQ ) tracks a cap-weighted index of companies engaged in Internet-related businesses from emerging and frontier markets. It is overweight in Chinese and other Asian companies, and is at the least an interesting play in the tech sector. Names such as Tencent, Alibaba, and Baidu (NASDAQ: BIDU ) make up a large portion of the portfolio, and no single holding is allowed to exceed 8% of the fund so as to reduce risk in a market riddled by explosive growth. Its approach to only select U.S.-listed companies that operate in emerging markets is intelligent, and helps to reduce exposure to “pink sheets,” or over-the-counter stocks. Its expense ratio is 0.86%, which again is a personal turn-off. That said, for those with a strong e-commerce thesis and an interest in emerging markets, this fund may be a solid long-term play.
XSD:
XSD is an interesting fund, using an equal-weighting methodology to construct a portfolio of companies operating in the semiconductor industry. It is fairly volatile and its small-cap tilt can offer an edge in a market prone to supply- and demand-based swings. State Street (NYSE: STT ), the fund’s issuer, offers an expense ratio of just 0.35%, which is quite excellent for a thematic ETF. Though not as cutting-edge as some of the above selections, it is a compelling play into companies that support infrastructure and development of new technologies.
HACK :
The ETFMG Prime Cyber Security ETF uses a similar methodology to ROBT. According to ETF.com : “HACK is the first ETF on the market that focuses on cybersecurity. The index it follows splits the industry into 2 types of firms: 1) those that create cybersecurity hardware and software; 2) those that provide cybersecurity as a service. Each of these segments is weighted proportionally by its respective market cap in comparison with the cumulative market cap of both segments.” It is highly liquid and offers smaller-cap exposure to a market that is set to grow at a 20% CAGR well into the next decade. The expense ratio of 0.64% is fair for the fund, and future performance should more than justify it.
SKYY :
The First Trust Cloud Computing ETF offers investors specialized exposure to the cloud computing industry. It is quite good at what it is intended to do, but the inherent low profitability of cloud computing makes it too speculative for my taste. The industry is threatened by low margins, conglomerates like Amazon (which offers excellent cloud computing services at little to no cost) and Microsoft, and even decentralized computing networks such as Ethereum. SKYY trades at over 58 times earnings, which I believe is unjustifiable especially given the high yields of data center REITs. The expense ratio is average, at 0.60%. I do not recommend this fund for those seeking broad exposure to technology and innovation.
ARKW:
Notable for being the top ETF performer in 2017, the ARK Web x.0 ETF is an actively managed fund that seeks to generate alpha through the shift away from hardware and towards software, including the Internet of Things, Internet currencies, machine learning, and various other hot industries. Its top ten holdings account for 46% of the portfolio, and include recognizable names like Tesla, Nvidia, Twitter, Tencent, and Amazon, among others. Because of this, it appears to be a momentum-oriented fund that rides the wave of speculation among both hedge funds and retail investors. It trades at over 300 times average earnings, which should give an indication of management’s growth-facing style. It has a low expense ratio of just 0.75%, which is excellent for an actively-managed fund.
Hercules Capital:
Hercules Capital (NASDAQ: HTGC ) is my unique play on the tech sector due to my belief that speculation is best left to those who are good at speculating. Hercules Capital provides senior secured loans to high-growth, innovative venture capital-backed companies in a variety of technology, life sciences, and sustainable and renewable technology industries. Management is exceptional, and the company is well-positioned for a rising rate environment having taken deleveraging efforts, refinanced high-interest debt at a much lower rate, and positioned the overwhelming majority of its portfolio at floating rates tied to LIBOR. It yields around 10% per share, and trades at around 10x earnings. For more in-depth coverage of Hercules Capital, I recommend reading this article by Achilles Research. I believe the company is excellent, and offers exposure to micro-cap companies that are not publicly traded and is successful in generating substantial return at a low risk -reflected by the average 20% premium to book value that shares trade at.
My Portfolio Here, we will construct an example portfolio for tech exposure going into the future. This is loosely based upon my personal thesis, risk tolerance, and subjective evaluations of management. It is intended to generate disproportionate risk-adjusted return over a long horizon through exposure to various funds, companies, and strategies in the information technology and automation sectors. That said, future results are not guaranteed, nor is it intended for the particularly risk-averse given its significant sector concentration and small- to mid-cap tilt.
The portfolio is designed to be simple and passive, allowing for a Bogle-esque management style and is optimized for investors with a time horizon of a decade or more. We begin with a straightforward 50% allocation to either VGT or FTEC - both broad market, low-fee ETFs intended to follow the returns of the underlying index. This enables us to roughly approximate the market, while allowing space for our own unique edge. Next, we will allocate 25% of our portfolio to RYT - the equal-weight S&P 500 technology fund, which gives our portfolio a much greater mid-cap tilt than otherwise would be allowed. History has shown that portfolios with a greater allocation towards equal-weighting methodologies or mid-cap companies may outperform in the long run, and RYT helps reduce overexposure to the explosive growth sometimes seen in this industry. Finally, we will give Hercules Capital a 25% position in our holdings, to offer exposure to venture-stage tech companies through competent and honest managers with industry expertise and support to their portfolio companies. HTGC will account for nearly all dividends in this portfolio, which will be reinvested after tax to allow for greater compounding gains and serve to lower our cost basis in the event of a market dip. For those seeking to gain exposure to a more niche sector in technology, I recommend whichever of the thematic ETFs discussed fits your thesis best, but to keep these core holdings at roughly their current allocations and not let a niche play exceed 15% of the entire portfolio. I have personally opted for ROBT due to its unique methodology and competitive expense ratio.
(Source: portfoliovisualizer.com )
We will use the Vanguard S&P 500 fund (NYSEARCA: VOO ) as our benchmark. Backtesting yields excellent results, with our sample portfolio generating annualized returns at nearly 12% from 2006 to the present, as compared to the benchmark’s CAGR of just 7.97%. The portfolio is rebalanced semi-annually, so as to avoid unjust concentration in a single holding. Alpha generated was nearly 3%, with a maximum peak-to-trough drawdown of 51%, comparable to that of the benchmark.

This is just the beginning of the worldwide tech boom. With our ever-increasing dependency on the Internet and mobile phones coupled with massive leaps in automation and genomics, shareholders of the future ought to be healthily rewarded for recognizing these trends early on. As always, my recommendations and advice are not guarantees of future performance and investors should always draw their own independent conclusions from further research.
Disclosure: I am/we are long HTGC, XLK, ROBT, RYT.
